title: The pilot with volunteers
scenario:
You are a sales operations manager at a software company with 60 sales reps. A vendor sells an AI assistant that writes first-draft emails to prospects. A regional director ran a quick pilot and now wants to roll the tool out to all reps.

You are asked to review the pilot before anyone signs. The exhibit shows the plan and the results.
exhibit:
AI email assistant pilot (made-up example data)

Plan
  Group A (tool): 12 reps who asked to try it. Period: December.
  Group B (no tool): the other 48 reps. Measured in September,
  because the December numbers were not ready.
  Planned stop: "when A is clearly ahead" (stopped after week 2).

Results per rep, per month (Group A: 2 weeks, scaled up to a month)
                          Group A    Group B
  Meetings booked          14.2       9.8
  Deals won                2.1        2.0
  Unsubscribe rate         1.9%       0.8%

No emails were read by a person.

questions.prompt: How should reps be put into the two groups in a fair pilot?

options.text: Let managers pick the reps they think will use the tool best.
options.explanation: Managers tend to pick strong reps, so Group A would be better even without the tool.

options.text: Draw names at random from all 60 reps, so chance decides who gets the tool.
options.explanation: Right. Random assignment makes the two groups alike, so the tool is the main difference. This is standard A/B practice.

options.text: Let reps who ask for the tool use it, and keep the rest as the control group.
options.explanation: This is what the pilot did. Keen volunteers may sell more with or without the tool.

options.text: Give the tool to the north region and keep the south region as the control.
options.explanation: Regions differ in market, customers and team. Those differences mix with the tool's effect.

questions.prompt: Group B was measured in September and Group A in December. What is the best fix?

options.text: Run both groups over the same weeks, so the season affects both alike.
options.explanation: Right. A season, a launch or a holiday then hits both groups, so the gap is easier to trust.

options.text: Compare Group A's December result with its own September result.
options.explanation: The season still changes between the two months, so the gap would show the calendar as much as the tool.

options.text: Add 10% to Group B's September numbers to allow for the busy season.
options.explanation: This is a guess. The real effect of the season is unknown.

options.text: Keep the plan, and write the month difference in a footnote.
options.explanation: A footnote tells the reader about the flaw but does not remove it.

questions.prompt: The plan says stop "when A is clearly ahead". What fits best?

options.text: Keep it. An early lead means the tool works, so stopping saves time.
options.explanation: An early lead can be luck, with 12 reps and 2 weeks. Anthropic says A/B tests take days or weeks and need enough traffic.

options.text: Stop at week 2 and ask the vendor to confirm the result.
options.explanation: The vendor does not set your success rules, and the early result is still thin.

options.text: Set the number of reps, the weeks and the main metric before the start.
options.explanation: Right. The rule is ours, and it fits Anthropic's point that A/B tests need enough time and traffic to be reliable.

options.text: Keep running until the tool is ahead on every number in the table.
options.explanation: Running until you like the result is also a bias. The end point must be fixed in advance.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the results is best supported, given the design problems?

options.text: Meetings are up 45%, so the tool should go to all 60 reps now.
options.explanation: The meeting gain is the headline, but the other two numbers do not support rolling out now.

options.text: Meetings rose, but deals did not and unsubscribes more than doubled.
options.explanation: Right. Meetings are up about 45%, but deals are up only 5% and unsubscribes are 2.4 times higher. The numbers are a weak signal, not a green light.

options.text: Group B is just as good, because deals won are nearly equal.
options.explanation: Deals are close, but the groups differ in design, so we can't make a firm claim about the tool either way.

options.text: The unsubscribe rate is small in both groups, so it can be ignored.
options.explanation: A rate that is 2.4 times higher is a warning about how prospects react. It is a guard number.
